video_caption: The video begins with an animation of Saturn and its rings, illuminated by a bright sun, set against a star-filled cosmic background, which then fades to white. This transitions to an animation of Earth, also bathed in light from a distant star, rotating in a nebulous deep space, fading out around the 0:15 mark. An orange-red background then displays contact information for "PROF. JIM CAFFEY" (PROF. JIM CAFFEY), including an email, LinkedIn, Facebook pages ("Science Professor Jim Caffey Page" (Science Professor Jim Caffey Page), "The Astronomers Group" (The Astronomers Group), "The Space Place Group" (The Space Place Group)), YouTube, and Twitter. A headshot of a smiling man with short brown hair, wearing a dark blue collared shirt, is shown on the left side of the screen. This transitions to a title slide reading "WELCOME TO 10-MINUTE ASTRONOMY! with PROFESSOR JIM CAFFEY" and "Episode 10 Chapter 6 Astronomical Instruments." Below this, two images are displayed: a vibrant, colorful depiction of "Comet Hyakutake - March 26, 1996" (Comet Hyakutake - March 26, 1996) on the left, and a long-exposure photograph of a telescope dome under a starry sky with a faint comet on the right. The man from the previous frame is overlaid in the bottom center, partially obscuring the images. At 0:28, the man, now wearing a grey polo shirt and a headset, is seen talking directly to the camera from his living room, with two small white dogs sitting near him on a patterned blanket. The background includes a couch, various framed pictures on the wall, and what appears to be a laptop. A "NEWS ALERT" (NEWS ALERT) box is visible in the bottom right, along with a Facebook notification. The screen then changes to a white background with a colorful border, displaying "ASTRONOMY" (ASTRONOMY) in green, and "Chapter 6 ASTRONOMICAL INSTRUMENTS PowerPoint Image Slideshow" (Chapter 6 ASTRONOMICAL INSTRUMENTS PowerPoint Image Slideshow) in black. An image of a blue book cover titled "Introduction to Astronomy" (Introduction to Astronomy) is centered on this slide. The man in the grey shirt is now relegated to a small window in the bottom right corner, continuing to speak and occasionally gesturing. The Facebook notification remains, and an "openstax" logo appears in the bottom right corner of the main slide. Finally, at 0:48, the main slide updates to "FIGURE 6.1" (FIGURE 6.1) with the "openstax" logo in the top right, showcasing an artist's impression of the "Hubble Space Telescope (HST)" (Hubble Space Telescope (HST)) above Earth, featuring its solar panels. The man in the small window continues to be visible.

A man with a beard and glasses, wearing a dark grey t-shirt, is visible in the bottom right corner, talking while looking at a presentation slide. From 0:03 to 0:11, the slide displays "FIGURE 6.1" and the "openstax" logo in the top right. The main content is an artist's impression of the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) orbiting Earth, with its rectangular solar panels visible on the left and right. Below the image, the text reads: "Hubble Space Telescope (HST). This artist's impression shows the Hubble above Earth, with the rectangular solar panels that provide it with power seen to the left and right." At 0:11, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 6.2," also with the "openstax" logo. This slide features three images labeled (a), (b), and (c), with detailed descriptions beneath them under the heading "Orion Region at Different Wavelengths." The man uses his mouse cursor to highlight specific areas in image (a), which shows a star constellation outlined with dotted yellow lines against a dark background. He first circles the bottom-left area, then moves the cursor to highlight the middle section of the constellation where three bright stars are aligned, which he identifies as "Orion's Belt" and the "Orion Nebula," as he continues to talk. The descriptive text for "FIGURE 6.2" explains that image (a) represents visible light, (b) shows X-rays, and (c) displays infrared radiation of the Orion region, with each image revealing different aspects of the celestial objects.

A man with glasses and a beard, wearing a dark collared shirt, is visible in the bottom right corner of the screen, speaking as he presents educational slides. From 0:02 to 0:15, the slide displays "FIGURE 6.3" (English: Figure 6.3) and the "openstax" logo at the top. The main content features two images: (a) an aerial view of Machu Picchu, ancient Incan ruins on a mountain, and (b) Stonehenge, a prehistoric stone circle in a grassy field. Below these images, the text reads "Two Pre-Telescopic Observatories." (English: Two Pre-Telescopic Observatories.) followed by descriptions: "(a) Machu Picchu is a fifteenth century Incan site located in Peru." (English: (a) Machu Picchu is a fifteenth century Incan site located in Peru.) and "(b) Stonehenge, a prehistoric site (3000-2000 BCE), is located in England. (credit a: modification of work by Allard Schmidt)" (English: (b) Stonehenge, a prehistoric site (3000-2000 BCE), is located in England. (credit a: modification of work by Allard Schmidt)). At 0:15, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 6.4" (English: Figure 6.4) with the same logo. This slide shows a diagram of "Formation of an Image by a Simple Lens." (English: Formation of an Image by a Simple Lens.), illustrating parallel light rays passing through a convex lens and converging at a "Focus" point, with a "Focal length" indicated. The accompanying text explains, "Parallel rays from a distant source are bent by the convex lens so that they all come together in a single place (the focus) to form an image." (English: Parallel rays from a distant source are bent by the convex lens so that they all come together in a single place (the focus) to form an image.) The man occasionally gestures with his right hand as he continues to speak.

In the video segment, a man with a beard and glasses, wearing a dark-colored shirt, is visible in the bottom right corner, looking at a screen and gesturing with his right hand. The main part of the screen displays two educational slides. The first slide (0:04-0:26) is titled "FIGURE 6.5" and shows two diagrams of telescopes. On the left is a "Refractor" with starlight entering a lens at the top, passing through the telescope, and exiting through another lens at the bottom to the eye. The man points at the lens as he explains. On the right is a "Reflector" where starlight enters an open top, hits a mirror at the bottom, reflects to a smaller mirror near the top opening, and then goes to the eye. The man points at the mirror and then the secondary mirror while explaining. Below the diagrams, text provides a description: "Refracting and Reflecting Telescopes. Light enters a refracting telescope through a lens at the upper end, which focuses the light near the bottom of the telescope. An eyepiece then magnifies the image so that it can be viewed by the eye, or a detector like a photographic plate can be placed at the focus. The upper end of a reflecting telescope is open, and the light passes through to the mirror located at the bottom of the telescope. The mirror then focuses the light at the top end, where it can be detected. Alternatively, as in this sketch, a second mirror may reflect the light to a position outside the telescope structure, where an observer can have easier access to it. Professional astronomers’ telescopes are more complicated than this, but they follow the same principles of reflection and refraction." The slide then transitions (0:26-0:32) to "FIGURE 6.6," which illustrates three different "Focus Arrangements for Reflecting Telescopes." These include "Prime focus" (light focuses at the top opening), "Newtonian focus" (light reflects off a secondary mirror to the side), and "Cassegrain focus" (light reflects off a secondary mirror and passes through a hole in the primary mirror at the bottom). Detailed explanatory text is also present below these diagrams, describing each focus type.

In the video segment, a man wearing a blue short-sleeved collared shirt is visible in the bottom right corner, actively speaking and gesturing with his right hand. From 0:03 to 0:10, a slide labeled "FIGURE 6.6" is shown, displaying three diagrams of reflecting telescopes with labels "Prime focus", "Newtonian focus", and "Cassegrain focus," illustrating different light ray paths, with a yellow circle briefly highlighting the secondary mirror in the "Newtonian focus" diagram. Below the diagrams, text explains "Focus Arrangements for Reflecting Telescopes," detailing how light is focused in each type of telescope. At 0:10, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 6.7," which presents an image of a massive, circular telescope mirror, surrounded by a metal ring, with two people in the background emphasizing its scale. A yellow circle briefly appears on the mirror's surface at 0:16, highlighting a spot. The accompanying text, "Large Telescope Mirror," identifies it as one of the primary mirrors of the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, named Yepun, after being recoated with aluminum, and notes its diameter is over 8 meters. At the very end of the segment, a brief beeping sound is audible.

A male presenter with a beard and glasses, wearing a dark shirt, is visible in the bottom right corner of the screen, speaking throughout the segment. The main content of the video displays three different images related to telescopes, each with a "FIGURE" number in the top left and an "openstax" logo in the top right.

From 00:00 to 00:06, "FIGURE 6.7" is shown, displaying a "Large Telescope Mirror." The image features a massive, circular, silvery telescope mirror, described as "Yepun," over 8 meters in diameter, mounted on an orange structure with wheels or tracks inside a workshop. A person in a blue shirt is standing near the mirror's base. The accompanying text reads: "Large Telescope Mirror. This image shows one of the primary mirrors of the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, named Yepun, just after it was recoated with aluminum. The mirror is a little over 8 meters in diameter. (credit: ESO/G. Huedephol)". A yellow circle briefly highlights a section of the mirror and then the person near it.

From 00:06 to 00:26, "FIGURE 6.8" is displayed, presenting two images side-by-side under the title "Modern Reflecting Telescopes." The left image (a) shows the interior of the Palomar 5-meter reflector (Hale telescope), with a large cylindrical component pointing upward, surrounded by intricate mounting structures. The right image (b) depicts the interior of the Gemini North 8-meter telescope, featuring a substantial blue base and white supporting trusses. The descriptive text states: "(a) The Palomar 5-meter reflector: The Hale telescope on Palomar Mountain has a complex mounting structure that enables the telescope (in the open "tube" pointing upward in this photo) to swing easily into any position. (b) The Gemini North 8-meter telescope: The Gemini North mirror has a larger area than the Palomar mirror, but note how much less massive the whole instrument seems. (credit a: modification of work by Caltech/Palomar Observatory; credit b: modification of work by Gemini Observatory/AURA)". A yellow circle highlights elements within both telescope images and then the credit line.

From 00:26 to 00:33, "FIGURE 6.9" is shown, featuring a single image titled "Thirty-Six Eyes Are Better Than One." This image provides an overhead view into the 10-meter Keck telescope, revealing its primary mirror composed of 36 hexagonal segments fitted together. A cylindrical instrument is suspended above the center of this segmented mirror. The accompanying text explains: "Thirty-Six Eyes Are Better Than One. The mirror of the 10-meter Keck telescope is composed of 36 hexagonal sections. (credit: NASA)".

The video segment opens with a slide titled "FIGURE 6.9" and the "openstax" logo. On the left, a black and white image displays the interior of a large telescope, featuring a central structure and numerous hexagonal mirror segments forming a primary mirror. The accompanying text on the right, in green, reads "Thirty-Six Eyes Are Better Than One." (meaning that using multiple smaller mirrors is more effective than one large mirror). Below that, the text states, "The mirror of the 10-meter Keck telescope is composed of 36 hexagonal sections. (credit: NASA)". A man with short dark hair, glasses, and a beard, wearing a dark short-sleeved shirt, is visible in the bottom right corner, looking at the screen and talking, occasionally gesturing with his right hand. He uses a yellow cursor to point at the mirror segments on the slide. His background shows shelves filled with books. At 0:16, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 6.10," still featuring the "openstax" logo. The left side of the new slide displays text in green: "George Ellery Hale (1868–1938)." Below this, the black text describes Hale's contributions: "Hale’s work led to the construction of several major telescopes, including the 40-inch refracting telescope at Yerkes Observatory, and three reflecting telescopes: the 60-inch Hale and 100-inch Hooker telescopes at Mount Wilson Observatory, and the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory." On the right, a black and white portrait of George Ellery Hale, a man with dark hair, a mustache, and glasses, dressed in a suit and tie, is shown. The man in the dark shirt continues to look at the screen and talk, maintaining a neutral to slightly smiling expression.

The video segment features a male presenter in the lower right corner, with short dark hair, a mustache, and glasses, wearing a short-sleeved casual shirt, speaking while presenting a slideshow. From 0:02 to 0:07, the slide shows a black and white portrait of a man in a suit, identified by the text "George Ellery Hale (1868-1938). Hale's work led to the construction of several major telescopes, including the 40-inch refracting telescope at Yerkes Observatory, and three reflecting telescopes: the 60-inch Hale and 100-inch Hooker telescopes at Mount Wilson Observatory, and the 200-inch Hale Telescope at Palomar Observatory." (This text provides biographical information about George Ellery Hale and lists major telescopes he helped construct). A yellow circle briefly highlights the portrait's chest area at 0:06. At 0:07, the slide changes to "FIGURE 6.11" with the text "World’s Largest Refractor. The Yerkes 40-inch (1-meter) telescope." (This identifies the image as the Yerkes telescope, the largest refracting telescope, and states its size). The accompanying image is a wide-angle shot inside an observatory dome, showing a massive white telescope tube mounted on a blue structure, extending upwards towards the ribbed white ceiling of the dome. A small blue circle appears briefly at the bottom center of the screen at 0:19. The slide then transitions at 0:20 to "FIGURE 6.12" with the text "High and Dry Site. Cerro Paranal, a mountain summit 2.7 kilometers above sea level in Chile’s Atacama Desert, is the site of the European Southern Observatory’s Very Large Telescope. This photograph shows the four 8-meter telescope buildings on the site and vividly illustrates that astronomers prefer high, dry sites for their instruments. The 4.1-meter Visible and Infrared Survey Telescope for Astronomy (VISTA) can be seen in the distance on the next mountain peak. (credit: ESO)" (This text describes the location and rationale for the Cerro Paranal observatory in the Atacama Desert, mentioning the Very Large Telescope and VISTA). The image displays an aerial view of an observatory complex with multiple white domed buildings on a barren, reddish-brown mountain peak, surrounded by a dry, arid, mountainous landscape under a hazy sky. A yellow circle briefly highlights the mountain peak at 0:26. Throughout, the "openstax" logo is visible in the top left corner.

The video segment showcases several figures related to astronomical observation, presented on a white slide with "FIGURE" titles and "openstax" branding, while a man with a gray shirt, glasses, and a beard is visible in the bottom right corner, seemingly recording a lecture or presentation. The first image (00:01-00:10), titled "FIGURE 6.12 High and Dry Site," displays an aerial view of the Cerro Paranal mountain summit in Chile's Atacama Desert, featuring four large 8-meter telescope buildings of the European Southern Observatory's Very Large Telescope, with a smaller 4.1-meter VISTA telescope visible on a distant peak, illustrating the preference for high, dry locations for observatories. The second image (00:10-00:36), titled "FIGURE 6.13 Power of Adaptive Optics," shows a remarkably clear, banded image of the planet Jupiter against a black background, highlighting the effectiveness of adaptive optics in removing atmospheric blurring, with a yellow cursor briefly circling part of Jupiter. The third image (00:36-00:56), titled "FIGURE 6.14 Charge-Coupled Devices (CCDs)," presents two sub-images: (a) a close-up of a silicon wafer containing multiple square CCD chips held by a hand, and (b) a person in a cleanroom working on a large matrix of these CCDs, which form part of the Kepler telescope, with a yellow cursor briefly highlighting one of the CCDs in sub-image (a). The fourth image (00:56-01:09), titled "FIGURE 6.15 Infrared Eyes," compares two images of a man holding a black plastic bag: the left shows him in visible light with the bag obscuring his hands, while the right shows an infrared image where the bag is transparent, revealing his heat-emitting hands through it, with a yellow cursor circling his hands in the infrared image. The final image (01:09-01:24), titled "FIGURE 6.16 Prism Spectrometer," displays a detailed diagram illustrating how a telescope focuses light onto a slit, which then passes through a collimating lens and a prism, splitting the light into its constituent colors (red, green, violet) to form a spectrum that is recorded by a camera lens onto a photographic plate or CCD, with a yellow cursor tracing the path of the light through the prism.

The video displays a series of educational slides, each featuring a black-and-white or color image with accompanying text, while a man in a dark blue t-shirt and glasses is visible in a small video frame in the bottom right corner, looking at the camera and speaking. The first slide, labeled "FIGURE 6.17," shows a black-and-white photograph of the "First Radio Telescope," an array of simple, angular wooden or metal structures arranged in an open, grassy field, with a person standing near them. The text explains, "This rotating radio antenna was used by Jansky in his serendipitous discovery of radio radiation from the Milky Way." The next slide, "FIGURE 6.18," presents a "Radio Image," a vibrant, false-color image against a dark blue background, depicting two large, amorphous cloud-like regions in shades of yellow, orange, red, and light blue, with a small bright dot and a faint streak connecting them in the center. The text clarifies, "This image has been constructed of radio observations at the Very Large Array of a galaxy called Cygnus A. Colors have been added to help the eye sort out regions of different radio intensities. Red regions are the most intense, blue the least. The visible galaxy would be a small dot in the center of the image. The radio image reveals jets of expelled material (more than 160,000 light-years long) on either side of the galaxy. (credit: NRAO/AUI)." Finally, "FIGURE 6.19" showcases a color photograph of the "Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope," a massive, white, fully steerable dish antenna set against a backdrop of rolling hills with colorful autumn foliage under a sky with white clouds. The accompanying text states, "This fully steerable radio telescope in West Virginia went into operation in August 2000. Its dish is about 100 meters across. (credit: modification of work by 'b3nscott'/Flickr)."

A man with a dark beard and short dark hair, wearing a patterned collared shirt, is seated in the bottom right corner of the screen, speaking and gesturing towards the presentation slides. Behind him is a bookshelf. The video shows a series of four presentation slides, each displaying a different image and accompanying text, with "FIGURE" and a number in green at the top left and an "openstax" logo at the top right. The first slide (0:00-0:08), "FIGURE 6.19," features an image of the Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope, a large white steerable radio telescope dish set against a backdrop of autumn-colored mountains and a cloudy sky. The text below states: "Robert C. Byrd Green Bank Telescope. This fully steerable radio telescope in West Virginia went into operation in August 2000. Its dish is about 100 meters across. (credit: modification of work by “b3nscott”/Flickr)." The second slide (0:08-0:17), "FIGURE 6.20," presents a panoramic night image of numerous radio telescope dishes under a starry sky with the Milky Way visible. The accompanying text reads: "Atacama Large Millimeter/Submillimeter Array (ALMA). Located in the Atacama Desert of Northern Chile, ALMA currently provides the highest resolution for radio observations. (credit: ESO/S. Guisard)." The third slide (0:17-0:31), "FIGURE 6.21," displays a stylized image of the Earth, seen from space with North and South America visible, marked with ten small black cross-shaped antenna locations spread across the United States. The text beneath explains: "Very Long Baseline Array. This map shows the distribution of 10 antennas that constitute an array of radio telescopes stretching across the United States and its territories." The fourth slide (0:31-0:44), "FIGURE 6.22," shows an aerial view of the Arecibo Observatory in Puerto Rico, featuring a massive circular radio dish nestled within a natural valley, surrounded by dense green foliage, with three large support towers. The text below identifies it as: "Largest Radio and Radar Dish. The Arecibo Observatory, with its 1000-foot radio dish-filling valley in Puerto Rico, is part of the National Astronomy and Ionosphere Center, operated by SRI International, USRA, and UMET under a cooperative agreement with the National Science Foundation. (credit: National Astronomy and Ionosphere Center, Cornell U., NSF)." The final slide (0:44-0:46), "FIGURE 6.23," shows a close-up side view of a white aircraft (Boeing 747SP) with a section of its fuselage open, revealing a large telescope mirror inside. The text "N747NA" is visible on the plane. The accompanying text states: "Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA). SOFIA allows observations to be made above most of Earth’s atmospheric water vapor. (credit: NASA)."

The video opens with a slide titled "FIGURE 6.23" showing a white airplane with "N747NA" printed on its tail, flying in a blue sky. A large rectangular opening on the side of its fuselage reveals a complex, metallic instrument, identified by the green caption below as "Stratospheric Observatory for Infrared Astronomy (SOFIA)," which allows observations above Earth's atmospheric water vapor. In the bottom right corner, a man with a beard and glasses, wearing a dark blue top, is visible, speaking. At 00:14, the slide transitions to "FIGURE 6.24," displaying three vibrant, multi-colored nebula images side-by-side: "Flame nebula," "Cassiopeia A," and "Helix nebula." A detailed green caption beneath these images explains they are infrared observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope, highlighting star formation, a supernova remnant, and an old star losing its outer shell, with colors chosen to indicate composition and temperature. The man in the bottom right corner continues to speak throughout the segment.

A man with a beard, wearing a blue t-shirt, is visible in the bottom right corner of the video frame, speaking as he presents a series of slides. The first slide, titled "FIGURE 6.24", displays three infrared images from the Spitzer Space Telescope: on the left, a "Flame nebula" (a region of star formation, a dense cloud of gas and dust that glows brightly); in the center, "Cassiopeia A" (the remnant of an exploded star, depicted with swirling red, orange, yellow, and blue gases); and on the right, a "Helix nebula" (a region where an old star is losing its outer shell, shown as a vibrant blue and pink eye-like structure). Below these images, a text block reads: "Observations from the Spitzer Space Telescope (SST). These Infrared Images—a region of star formation, the remnant of an exploded star, and a region where an old star is losing its outer shell—show just a few of the observations made and transmitted back to Earth from the SST. Since our eyes are not sensitive to infrared rays, we don’t perceive colors from them. The colors in these images have been selected by astronomers to highlight details like the composition or temperature in these regions. (credit: 'Flame Nebula': modification of work by NASA (X-Ray: NASA/CXC/PSU/K. Getman, E. Feigelson, M. Kuhn & the MYSTIX Team; Infrared: NASA/JPL-Caltech); credit: 'Cassiopeia A': modification of work by NASA/JPL-Caltech; credit: 'Helix Nebula': modification of work by NASA/JPL-Caltech)." The second slide, "FIGURE 6.25", features a vast image titled "Hubble Ultra-Deep Field (HUDF)", showcasing countless distant galaxies and stars against a black backdrop, with a description below stating: "The Hubble Space Telescope has provided an image of a specific region of space built from data collected between September 24, 2003, and January 16, 2004. These data allow us to search for galaxies that existed approximately 13 billion years ago. (credit: modification of work by NASA)." The third slide, "FIGURE 6.26", shows an image of the "Chandra X-Ray Satellite" orbiting in space, with a colorful nebula in the background, accompanied by text: "Chandra, the world's most powerful X-ray telescope, was developed by NASA and launched in July 1999. (credit: modification of work by NASA)." The final slide, "FIGURE 6.27", presents an image of the "James Webb Space Telescope (JWST)" mirrors undergoing cryogenic testing, with two technicians in protective suits visible within the image, and explanatory text: "This image shows some of the mirrors of the JWST as they underwent cryogenic testing. The mirrors were exposed to extreme temperatures in order to gather accurate measurements on changes in their shape as they heated and cooled. (credit: NASA/MSFC/David Higginbotham/Emmett Given)." All slides consistently feature the "openstax" logo in the top right corner.

The video begins with a presentation slide (Figure 6.27) displaying an image of the hexagonal mirrors of the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) undergoing cryogenic testing. Text on the slide reads, "James Webb Space Telescope (JWST). This image shows some of the mirrors of the JWST as they underwent cryogenic testing. The mirrors were exposed to extreme temperatures in order to gather accurate measurements on changes in their shape as they heated and cooled. (credit: NASA/MSFC/David Higginbotham/Emmett Given)." A small inset video at the bottom right shows a man in a dark green hooded sweatshirt looking at the slide and speaking. The scene then transitions to another presentation slide (Figure 6.28), which is an artist's conception of the European Extremely Large Telescope (ELT) situated in a desert landscape. The accompanying text states, "Artist's Conception of the European Extremely Large Telescope. The primary mirror in this telescope is 39.3 meters across. The telescope is under construction in the Atacama Desert in Northern Chile. (credit: ESO/L. Calçada)." The man continues to speak in the small window. Next, a white slide with an OpenStax logo and copyright information is shown, reading, "This OpenStax ancillary resource is © Rice University under a CC-BY 4.0 International license; it may be reproduced or modified but must be attributed to OpenStax, Rice University and any changes must be noted." Finally, the video cuts to a full-screen view of the man, now wearing a maroon hoodie with a white "M" and "Missouri" logo and a headset with a microphone. He has short, light brown hair and a beard, and is smiling as he speaks directly to the camera. His room's background features various posters, including what appears to be a space-themed image and one with a red umbrella, along with colorful string lights and a ceiling fan. As he speaks, text captions appear at the bottom of the screen: "Well did you enjoy that episode of 10 minute ...", "astronomy?", "If so check out all the other...", "videos and that playlist for 10 minute astronomy and other...", "videos on my channel and then hit the subscribe...", "button right there.", "Thanks." He gestures with his right hand, pointing towards the lower right corner of the screen as he mentions the subscribe button.
